utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom, this is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, everybody. I notice that for the record that all the accused are here, representation is exactly as it was yesterday except the seating is different. Good morning, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I leave him in your hands. Remember that it's Friday, the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges. Good morning colleagues in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When we left off yesterday, sir, you were telling us that when you had this conversation with Dragan Obrenovic at the forward command post on the 16th of July, he did not say anything about an alleged conversation he would have had with an elderly member of the 4th Battalion on 15 July and nor that he possessed any information that Drago Nikolic was involved in the killing of prisoners at Orahovac. That was at page 31386 to 31387. In your very last answer, you said the following, and I quote: "I would have expected him to tell me that, but since he did not do this and I don't know for what reason, perhaps he really did not know and he had nothing to do with it. It was probably the reason why he didn't mention it." Now, if I can have in e-court 3D7D86, please. I'd like to have page 5 in English, so the document that will appear before you -- maybe I can say that number over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was go to tell you to ask you to wait and be patient a little bit. Do you need the number again? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 3D7D86. And that is the statement of facts which which accompanied the guilty plea of Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I will refer to a segment of the statement of facts provided by Dragan Obrenovic and I quote from paragraph 34. And that's page 5 in English: "He mentioned the following: Ristic told me that Milorad Trbic had called him from Orahovac school where the prisoners were being kept and asked for help. Ristic then sent about eight men to Orahovac as reinforcements to assist Trbic in guarding the prisoners."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we on the same page, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me verify, Judge. I have paragraph 34, line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is we don't have -- the text that we have is -- the numbers are not -- sorry, the paragraphs are not numbered. So we have to go through each one of them to try and see, and we don't know where that starts with those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's on page 5 in English, according to the document that I have here which is the 3D7D86 page 5, and the paragraph begins with, "We went directly to the command of the 4th Battalion," beginning of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The end of that page, last paragraph of that page. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We have to go to page 6 for the part that I was referring to. I apologise for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is okay. It is right in the middle in B/C/S, it's right in the middle of the page. It starts, "otisli smo direktno," but very soon we'll have to go to the next page in English. Anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In English we have to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly. All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It starts at the fourth line with: "Ristic told me."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So sir, I will read this segment over again. "Ristic told me that Milorad Trbic had called him from Orahovac school where the prisoners were being kept and asked for help. Ristic then sent about eight men to Orahovac as re-enforcements to assist Trbic in guarding the prisoners. Ristic said he did not know at that stage about the killing of prisoners at Orahovac, but learnt about it when he visited the site early in the evening of the 14th July. He said that he found his men guarding prisoners in the gymnasium of the school at Orahovac and that the execution of prisoners had already commenced in the nearby location. He lined up his men and was about to take them away, when Drago Nikolic stopped him. Drago Nikolic said that if the men stayed, they would all be issued with new uniforms by Captain Milosevic from rear services. Lazar Ristic spoke of other soldiers there in camouflage uniform from another location and he was not clear where they were from." I take it, sir, you are familiar with the statement of facts from Dragan Obrenovic, and we also referred to that statement of facts yesterday. It's my understanding, however, that during your conversation with Obrenovic at the forward command post, he did not tell you anything about this alleged conversation with Lazar Ristic on 15 July at the 4th Battalion command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you were in this courtroom when Lazar Ristic appeared as a witness and denied having such a conversation at the 4th Battalion command with Dragan Obrenovic, so I take it that when Lazar Ristic testified, you weren't surprised by him denying ever having that conversation.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if Obrenovic would have had such a conversation with Lazar Ristic, and if, at that time, he did have information that Drago Nikolic and Milorad Trbic were involved in the guarding of prisoners at Orahovac, would you have expected him at the time to tell you when you asked if anyone from the Zvornik Brigade was involved?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected him to tell me everything that he knew regarding these events including whether anyone from the Zvornik Brigade took part in those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: One last question concerning your conversation with Obrenovic. Yesterday, when I asked you whether Obrenovic told you where Drago Nikolic was when Obrenovic allegedly obtained information from him on 13 July, your answer was, and I quote: "... and I don't think he told me where Drago Nikolic was and whether he called him or whether he had any personal contact with him." If I can add ... one moment, please. The question I put to you at that time, just to recall, was did Obrenovic tell you where Drago Nikolic was when he conveyed this information to him. If I can have in e-court please 7D1154, page 3 in English and page 4 in B/C/S. Sir, this document that will appear before you is the investigative note to file compiled by Eileen Gilleece, which was discussed in detail during your examination-in-chief two days ago. I draw your attention to the last paragraph on this page which reads as follows: "Drago Nikolic was the chief of security for the Zvornik Brigade and the duty officer for the forward command post replaced by Major Galic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to go --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Again we have the wrong page? I apologise. I said page 3 in English, please and page 4 in B/C/S. I apologise. I will look again. On the last page, page 3, last paragraph. Here we are. So you see the last -- in English it's the last paragraph and in the -- in your language, it's the fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The sentence I was referring to is: "Drago Nikolic was the chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade and the duty officer for the forward command post replaced by Major Galic." Sir, on the basis of the information or the -- your last answer, about what Major Obrenovic told you during that conversation, I suggest to you that this was not information that was communicated to you by Obrenovic on 16 July, and that, in fact, this is something you learned for the first time when you read the Butler report before having this meeting with Eileen Gilleece. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I explained how the security organ was mentioned at all and that Zivanovic got involved. When he mentioned certain names, I explained which posts they held. I don't remember at all mentioning the whereabouts of Drago, whether it was at the IKM or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the specific information included in this paragraph where it says, "Replaced by Major Galic," this is not something you were familiar with at the time you met Eileen Gilleece; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read Mr. Butler's report. Whether this was included in this report or not, but to me this was entirely irrelevant information, whether he was at the IKM and whether Mr. Galic had replaced him, so this made no impression on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, I appreciate that's very useful, but I just need to clarify this to ensure that we are -- I just want to know that this information which is included there is not something that you knew or that you were ever informed of in July of 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, you're right. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to clarify. I move to a different topic of my cross-examination, and I would like to ask you a few questions concerning your military background. If I can have in e-court please P372, page 1 in both languages. Sir, you will recognise this document which was also shown to you during your examination in chief and it has to do with your personal information on -- or with respect to your military career. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to see this document but it seems that somebody else had filled in this form. This is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you quickly glance over the information that is included in this document -- now my understanding it was shown to you during your examination-in-chief but we'll -- I have just a few questions concerning this document. First, let's go to paragraph 10 where it says that you joined the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, on 30 July, 1982. Now that's correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We finished the military academy in July, and we were given ranks of second-lieutenant. I think it was mid-July, between the 18th and the 20th, and this is the period that is calculated as the date of joining the army, only later on, I was given a specific post and a duty station in Ljubljana in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So just to -- for the sake of clarity, first you go to military academy and then you join the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it says that at paragraph 9, that you spent 4.6 years at the military academy and that's the normal stay, it's a five-year course; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I spent four years. I don't know who wrote this 4.6, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, during your examination-in-chief on 27 January, you confirmed that you were promoted to lieutenant in July of 1983, to captain in 1987, and to captain first class in 1991. This was at transcript page 30668, line 24 to page 30669, line 3 on 27 January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to this document, it also says at paragraph 11 that you distinguish yourself as a JNA officer in 1989 and 1991. Would I be right in saying that this means that you obtained outstanding evaluation reports on both occasions?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly when my official appraisal took place, but generally it was done every four years; and I was familiar with every official appraisal because I had to sign it as taking a note of it. And probably this outstanding appraisal was given to me by Battalion Commander Vahid Karavelic, who was later commander of the BH army 1st Corps in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, is it at that time on 1 June 1992 that you officially switched from the JNA to the VRS as we see in paragraph 12 of this document?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was formally on the register of the VJ, formerly the JNA. My wartime assignment was in the Army of Republika Srpska. I don't remember the exact date, but I do know that the orders about our transfer followed only much later which is to say after we had actually been transferred. That is why I really cannot remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I appreciate this. Now if we look at paragraph 7, we say the dates of your promotions to major, 7 January 1993; to lieutenant-colonel, 31 May 1994; and to colonel on 31 December 1995. I'm not so much interested in the dates on which you were promoted but more so in the fact that it says that these promotions were extraordinary promotions. What does that mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law on the army, it specifies exactly how long each officer should remain with a certain rank provided he is assigned to an appropriate post and that he achieved an appropriate appraisal. It varies between three, four, and seven years. Each promotion that is being effected before that time elapsed is considered as extraordinary promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So in common language, those are promotions which come faster than the normal required time for the next rank.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And only the very best officers get such promotions.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how things are supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And extraordinary promotions are also given to officers who receive outstanding evaluation reports; are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, only under the law he held the rank for a shorter time than someone who had lower evaluation. I remember a captain who had an outstanding evaluation who was promoted after a shorter period of time, but it doesn't guarantee that it will happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I take it that you are familiar that on the basis of your experience, that in the military, from the time that you are a junior officer, if your superiors see the potential in you to reach the higher ranks in the army, you become what is known as a streamer and then you get a series of quick promotions. Are you familiar with that normal way of doing in the military?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was very specific in the JNA. One didn't only need general quality and capacity and training and good performance for someone to achieve speedy promotions, there were other things that we, at that time, called the ethnic key and also certain political appropriateness and achievements in the sphere of politics. It could have happened that for a variety of reasons, certain officers, thanks to their good qualities, could have "represented" a professional threat to someone else and therefore didn't receive promotions. However, war is an opportunity to test everyone's qualities, both human qualities and professional qualities including valour, bravery, et cetera. That is why as the law says, in wartime, the president of the republic can promote an ordinary private to a general because these are extraordinary circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very useful, and that fits into my next questions where all of your extraordinary promotions you obtained in the VRS, this happened during the war?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it can be concluded that during the war, you were regarded by your superiors as an outstanding officer?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to my arrival in the Zvornik Brigade, my superiors probably did not have a complete picture of my work and sufficient information about my quality. When I arrived in Zvornik, however, after only 10 or 15 days I was promoted to the rank of major for a single reason. This was a large brigade. The previous commanders had been lieutenant-colonels, and one of them had been a major and that milieu needed a certain authority which the rank of major gave me, both among the men and my peers. This was an expression of the needs, the requirements of the time, not something due to my special qualities because I'd only been there for some 10 or 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I was referring sir more to your -- what your superiors saw in you throughout the war, and I will refer to one example and that is when General Krstic testified during his trial, that was at page 6312, lines 7 to 10 on 20 October 2000, he said you were, and I quote: "The best brigade commander in the Drina Corps, one of the best commanders amongst his peers in the army as a whole, a professional soldier in every sense of the word." Do you agree with General Krstic's assessment which he said during his trial?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had the right to evaluate my work because he was my superior. I agree with that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now one thing I'm curious about, however, is your military education, in other words, whether and when you attended the career courses which are usually a prerequisite before getting certain promotions. If I begin with the command and staff academy. You said in your testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Bourgon, initially I forgot to put on record that we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 business. Judge Stole couldn't be with us this morning. The other thing is before you proceed with this line of questions, what are you seeking to prove?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's coming very quickly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We were talking about, sir, the command and staff academy, and you said in your testimony that you attended the first 20 days of the command and staff academy but that you did not complete the course due to wartime obligations. That was at page 30673 on 27 January; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The course mentioned here was the regular schooling which lasted for two years at the time. There were also courses for company commanders and battalion commanders. The regular schooling in the JNA covered the military academy, the staff command, the command and staff academy and some similar schools, and also the school of national defence or the war school. All these were forms of regular schooling. In addition to this, in the course of one's service in the JNA, there was a special plan of training for officers which was implemented on a monthly basis. Every officer was duty-bound to undertake continuous education in the course of his service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, my first question in this regard is: Did you ever complete the command and staff academy after the war at any time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the war, the generation which started its schooling together with me in 1991 had its schooling interrupted because of the war and continued again in 1993. I was invited back to the school, but the commander of the Main Staff did not approve my return to the school which is why I did not complete it. However, because I have a master of arts in sociology, I was given a VES, which is my military specialty which has the -- carries the same rank as the command and staff school. After the war, I tried to enroll again in that school, but again it was not approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My second question in this regard is those 20 days that you say you attended the staff command academy, now, I take it that this was in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And to which unit did you belong at the time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assistant commander for moral guidance and political guidance, and also I deputised with the battalion commander. That unit moved to Zenica, and from Zenica, I went to that school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the unit you were with just because this was my precise question was the 1st Motorised Battalion of the 14th Volunteer Brigade in the Ljubljana Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that was the unit commanded then by Vahid Karavelic, who you mentioned earlier before?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now those 20 days that you spent at the staff command academy is this information that should appear in your personal dossier at any place?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in my file, there should be orders showing that I was sent to school as well as the order that after the interruption of my schooling I was assigned to temporary work in the Uzice Corps or the 37th Corps as it was called to the 19th Mountain Brigade, and that should all be in my file. I think there were two copies in the file and one was always kept in the personnel department of the General Staff of the JNA in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Have you seen this information yourself in your personal records?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the order sending me to school and the one sending me to temporary work in the Uzice Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And have you seen your personal record here in The Hague since you arrived some three years ago?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw parts of that record and yesterday, I saw the remainder from my photograph as a second-lieutenant onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, that's information that I've been looking for, and I could not locate, so I will seek the assistance of your counsel to provide this information. We've been trying to get this from the Prosecution. We don't know if it exists or not, but I have a series of questions that were following; but I will wait until I see the documents before I put my questions to the witness on this particular issue. Sir, the staff and command academy, you will agree with me, is a prerequisite for promotions to the group of senior officer or higher officers as you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned a few moments ago one of the career courses which officers must attend before getting promoted to senior positions in the VRS would be the National Defence School; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this is the one-year course you mentioned during your testimony, the course you attended in Belgrade in 1997, but as you told us, you only graduated in January 1999 due to disciplinary proceedings which were instituted against you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, even though you only graduated from the National Defence School in January of 1999, you were nonetheless promoted to major-general on 28 June 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. First, I completed the war and then the war school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, you would agree with me that you really have to be a very good officer in order to be promoted to the rank of major-general before having attended or completed the career courses such as the National Defence School.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If someone has a wide choice to promote someone to that rank and appoint him to a certain duty, and if there is a lot of competition, then it's very difficult. If the choice is very limited, then even someone who doesn't fulfill all the conditions can be promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of yourself being a very good officer during the war, I'd like to refer to the testimony of Milenko Ljubicic, who testified at page 11576 that you were an exceptionally strict commander, that you knew the job that you were doing very, very well, and you were an extremely good person; do you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to do my job in the best way I could, whether it was all good enough, well, probably it wasn't. My strictness was based, first of all, on strictness towards myself and then towards others. I was not stricter towards others than I was towards myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I refer to the testimony of Miodrag Dragutinovic, that was at pages 12639 and 12640, he testified that you had a lot of skill and knowledge about the unit command, and you took very seriously the orders you received from higher command. Do you agree with this assessment from Miodrag Dragutinovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I'm afraid I might be reactivated after all these questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And finally, you became a general in the Army of Yugoslavia and that was on 20 March 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, something you mentioned during your examination-in-chief that I'd like to look a bit into, and I'd like to know that during the war when you were a younger officer, I'd like to know, were you an ambitious man, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to refer to Napoleon saying that a soldier who one day doesn't want to become a general is a poor soldier. If that's ambition, well, I don't think I was more ambitious than you are, for example, it's a privilege to be a lawyer in this court, appear as counsel here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we come to the point because to be honest, I don't know what you think, but if you think that we are interested in all this, go ahead by all means. But I suggest to you to think different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your advice is noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you testified two days ago that when the president of Republika Srpska, Mrs. Plavsic selected you to become the assistant commander for morale, religious and legal affairs for the general staff, there were reports in the Belgrade media highlighting the fact that you were too ambitious. That was at transcript 31254. You said that you did not enjoy these reports. What truth was there to these reports, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I said, the authors wrote what they did. They wanted to challenge the credibility of new appointees to the General Staff. They wanted to challenge the credibility of the same people they had praised in wartime when they had to risk their lives, but now when someone was appointed to a similar duty as his predecessors he was not good enough. So this was all envy and competition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you probably recall that when Nebojsa Jeremic testified in this trial, I asked him about, or I comment in a statement he provided to the office of the Prosecution to the effect that you acted like a god in the brigade. That was at page 10444. Why would Jeremic say, in your opinion, that you acted like a god in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May God forgive me if I ever had such a thought. I am a mere mortal. I am not a god. How he came to that conclusion, I don't know. To the best of my understanding, Mr. Bourgon, I may be wrong, you were a soldier once and you know that the role of a commander is to invest his best efforts in getting his unit to perform its task. He may not always be successful. Sometimes one succeeds and sometimes one doesn't. They may have viewed me as a god because they are not religious people. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I heard, when preparing this case, comments from many of your former soldiers that you were not only an ambitious man, but that you were ready to sacrifice anything for your career including your men, which is why even though you lost many soldiers that way, you were always ready to fight outside of your own territory to show how good you are. Is there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon is giving evidence. What he heard in the preparation of this case has got nothing to do with anything Mr. Pandurevic should comment upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, do you wish to comment -- Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If this kind of thing is going to be thrown at any witness it should be specified where it's coming from and what it is because otherwise it really is absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has that convinced you to move to your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Not really, Mr. President. I think in cross-examination, if I have a foundation to ask a question and to ask whether it is true, whether Mr. Pandurevic feels that he was willing to sacrifice anything to his career, it is something that I'm entitled to explore in cross-examination because it will have to do with his decisions after that which I will challenge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you in a position to quote -- give proper indication of your source, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I've heard this from many former soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade, which I have interviewed in preparing for this case and he can tell us if there is any foundation to these comments that I've heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed and we suggest, again, that you go to the facts which are relevant to the case rather than this background information. If it continues like this, we are in agreement here that we will have to cut down on your 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that if there is one thing that you could not tolerate from anyone during the war, it would be anyone who would disseminate information which would tarnish your reputation; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I have to touch on your previous question. I did my very best to protect the lives of my men and to ensure that my soldiers had what they needed. These were reservists who did not understand the logic of warfare and the ways in which soldiers were used. They were local patriots. Had they carried out my orders and acted in ways described by certain individuals in this courtroom, and had everything been done the way they say it was, I would happily have had been a commander for another ten years, but that's not how it was. I could not prevent the dissemination of disinformation. There was a huge amount of disinformation coming from various sources. If every soldier did not see me next to him at the front line, he said I went to Loznica in Serbia and that I was sitting in a cafe. I would have had to have been seen by every soldier at every time everywhere because if they didn't see me in the brigade, they would start spreading rumours about me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, I appreciate this answer, and we'll come back to this later in my cross-examination but for now I would simply say that one of the reasons for which you testified the way you did concerning Drago Nikolic is that at some point during the war, he did make a report against you which you found out about; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this is about. If there is something like that, please jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will. But for now, I'd like to quickly turn to the issue of officer-like qualities, and as it was put to you by your counsel, you've been in the army all your life; and I'd like you to confirm whether you agree with me that trust and loyalty towards the chain of command is one of the most important, if not the most important value in the military profession.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should be in every army, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it's very important for a general to be able to trust his senior officers?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trust must exist. Without trust, there can be no successful work, but trust can be betrayed. I never used any other methods to obtain information important to me and my command, apart from the usual procedures envisaged by the rules of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it was very important for a brigade commander such as yourself during the war to trust your Chief of Staff, your assistant commanders, and your officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was responsible both to my superior and to my subordinates and associates. I was responsible to the local community. I had responsibility towards myself and also to my enemies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one of the areas, sir, where trust can be demonstrated between officers is in written communications; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, you will agree with me that a general must trust that what his brigade commanders will tell him in written communications such as a combat report, for example, is accurate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's logical that communication must go two ways, that there must be information coming from the top down and also from the bottom up. The flow of information from the top down is usually faster than the other way around. A subordinate always can either alter the information to make it look better that he sends up or he can send up accurate information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on this basis, sir, you will agree with me that when an officer drafts and sends a combat report, for example, it is critical that the information contained therein be as accurate as possible?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he usually writes down the information he has available because he, himself, gets information from the duty organs of subordinate units. When the information starts from the company up to battalion and then up to corps level, it arrives at various nodes where certain elements can be lost so that in the end, the information can appear quite different by the time it reaches the top. That's always a problem in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that you will agree with me that if a combat report does not contain accurate information, whether it was on purpose or simply because the officer sending the report does not have the right information, this can have disastrous consequences for the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can have consequences, whether disastrous or not so important depends on a particular situation. However, having information at one's disposal is essential in order to make the right assessment and reach the right decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you will also agree with me that if you found out that one of your officers deliberately sent you a combat report containing false information, you could no longer trust this officer thereafter; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't fully agree. I would undertake measures to make him write future reports as accurately as possible. If I lose trust at any point, I would have no choice other to dismiss this officer and give up on him. One has to work with people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, my question is quite straightforward: Did you ever tell General Krstic or any of your superior officers that on 16 July 1995, you deliberately sent to them a combat report concerning false information as you say you did?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't tell him that. He could have concluded that himself just like the visit by the team from the Main Staff and what was actually and really going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I take it then that General Krstic and the -- your senior officers at the time never got back to you saying that you had filed a false combat report on the 16th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was no discussion about that report. There were speedy developments. The situation in the Krajina was chaotic, and there was no discussion about that. However, speaking about true or false reports, I have to tell you about certain practice that was implemented both in the JNA and the VRS; and that is that an in addition to commander's reports about the same event, their assistants for security reports followed as a confirmation of whether this was true or not. When you mentioned my meeting with Mr. Semso in November 1993 in the presence of Mr. Drago Nikolic, I reported about this meeting, the corps command in my regular report whereas Drago, along his line of communication and reporting, informed the security administration of the main corps [as interpreted]. The corps command then asked me to send a special report about what had actually transpired and to address it to the Chief of the Main Staff of the corps [as interpreted]. I was really surprised at this request, and this is just one of the examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but we had some translation issues that are just going to confuse the issue. If you can see, we interchanged Main Staff of the corps, main corps, things I think that can be fixed simply enough, but I don't think they should sit in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Bourgon if you want to go through it now you can do so otherwise if you prefer you can do it later with the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll make one correction, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just at page 24, line 6 where it says main corps, I take it Mr. Pandurevic, you meant Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the English transcript in front of you, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So page 24, line 6, sir, where it says, "security administration of the main corps." Is that what you said, or can you clarify what you said exactly?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security administration of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at the end on the last line where you said, "Address it to the chief of the Main Staff of the corps," now that's not what you said, I take it.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent the report to the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps because probably Zivanovic was not that at the time, instead Colonel -- late Colonel Skocajic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I get to my point here because you said that I mentioned Semso Muminovic, I don't recall I did, but I will check my notes. My question is the following, and we'll get back to this when we get back to the events of the 16th of July, but I put to you that an officer of your calibre enjoying the absolute trust of your corps commander as we have seen, and aiming for the highest positions of the army, would never deliberately include false information in a combat report. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that, and I invite you to confirm that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I simply put it to you that your combat report of 16 July with respect to the information contained therein with the situation as it evolved on the ground was an accurate report and did not contain false information.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that four or five times, the corps and the Main Staff asked for reports and that some people were sent out to check the situation. The report was as I described it in my examination-in-chief, and I also believe that another protected witness spoke about this in a similar manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you agree with me that your report represented accurately the situation as it evolved in the field?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report reflected the situation as I believed would create the least consequences as a result of my actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But that's not my question, sir. I want to know whether the situation on the ground on 16 July was as you reported it in your interim combat report or whether you deliberately sent false information up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information was partly untrue, particularly the one relating to the loss of three trenches, that was not correct. The front-line had never been broken through at any point. Also, if I can remember, that everyone who passed through passed unarmed. That is not true. You can see it in the video footage who passed through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I further suggest to you, sir, this will be my last question on this topic, that your reason why you say what you said what you said during your testimony is to convince us is that you let the 28th Division cross your lines with their weapons on 16 July, not for humanitarian reasons, but rather because you wanted to save your brigade as a good commander should do if this is possible without compromising the ultimate mission he is entrusted with; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Saving lives and one's soldiers and that of the enemy's as well are humanitarian reasons. My task was to repel the breakthrough by the 28th Division. I wasn't able to do that, but I could have massacred the 28th Division. I could have pulled out my men from Baljkovica, let the 28th Division concentrate in the area, allow elements of the 2nd Corps to link up with them, and in the area of one square kilometre, cover 5.000 men with artillery fire and each shell would hit the target; and, therefore, I would have fulfilled my task completely. However, that's not what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back to that when we cover the events of 16 July, but I now move to a different topic. And I'd like to ask you a few questions concerning some of the evidence which was heard in this trial. Now, of course as a person accused in this case, you've been sitting in the courtroom for the testimony of all witnesses who appear before this Trial Chamber with the exception of one or two days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During your testimony, you mentioned that you also reviewed documents which had been given to you to prepare for your defence.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, in fact, you even mentioned, that was on page 30821, lines 23 to 24 that you were shown all documents on the EDS system; do you recall saying this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all documents were shown to me. What I received in an electronic form from the EDS was what I reviewed, but I don't think it was a complete set. I've -- I see that you are announcing some documents that I haven't seen before, and I believe it was impossible to go through all of them in the period of time that I had at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't think I am announcing such documents on my list, but if I do, I will speak to your counsel at the break. Now, you are familiar with all of what the witnesses in this case have said and also with the witnesses that were not called by the Prosecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard all the testimony given here. I don't remember, however, all the details of each testimony, and I don't know what the witnesses who haven't appeared here told to the OTP. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question was actually poorly put to you. I'm not talking about witnesses who weren't called, but you read statements obtained by the Office of the Prosecution from persons who did not testify in this trial; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a number of statements, whether that's a full set, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you are familiar with the documents both with have been discussed in this courtroom and those which you received which were not admitted in evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is so ambiguous, I don't know what documents you are referring to. I reviewed a huge number of documents that were put on e-court and shown here including those who haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's -- that was my question, so I take it that you understood it. But all of this evidence, sir, whether coming from witnesses or from persons who were to be witnesses or documents, I take it that you have had an opportunity to discuss these documents with your defence team?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed many things, primarily those that we thought to be of vital importance to our approach to this case, but of course we didn't discuss each and every document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I don't want to get into the details of any discussion, that's not my purpose, but would I be right in saying that you, yourself, have been active in the preparation of your defence?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was active. I did a lot of work on my own. That was because I believed that I have to do everything in my capacity regardless of the outcome of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And for example, you mentioned that you met with your expert witness, Bosko Antic; and you said that you gave him some general guidance before he set out on his mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that you actually drafted some questions which were put to witnesses during this trial?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which witness you are having in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you draft questions in order to help your defence team put your case forward before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For each witness, I assisted my defence team and their preparations by reviewing documents, by offering my own interpretations and professional expert explanations, by providing the facts that I knew. However, the drafting and the formulating of questions in the form that is permissible in this courtroom is something to be done by a professional defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And without getting into the details of any particular conversation you had with your defence team, is it correct to say that in general, your defence was and is being presented pursuant to your instructions?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that's the point of cooperation in defence cases. Whenever my defence team managed to persuade me something, I never interfered any longer with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what I'm curious about is that if and when some evidence was heard that you disagreed with, I take it that you made a point of raising these issues with your defence team?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have disagreed with evidence, but I couldn't change evidence. I could have told them where we had interpretation of facts and where we had actual facts because there is a huge difference between a fact and an interpretation of facts as someone who took part in events can speak about the facts. Someone else can talk about interpretation of facts based on the knowledge or rather second-hand knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, did you hear any evidence, testimony, or see documents admitted in this trial which you believed to be not true or not accurate?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many documents were admitted into evidence in this court. For a certain period of time, I tried to keep track of those documents but then I realised it was a futile effort, and I gave up. Whether all these documents are true and correct, I honestly don't know. But we discussed each and every document through cross-examination here, and I'm referring to the documents that we were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how about witness testimony, did you hear any witnesses in this courtroom where you went back to your room and you thought this evidence is not true?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If witness testimonies were contrary to what I know and I believe that was true, then I thought that this witness didn't speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what did you do when this was the case? How did you react?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we would analyse these specific testimonies, we would use documents, and by analysing the contents and the -- making comparisons with other testimonies and other documents, we would arrive at certain conclusions and attempt to arrive at the truth. You are now asking me about some expert procedures that you are more familiar with than I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I notice it's getting to the break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But I'm also, just for the record, some of these questions are obviously taking the witness into the area of attorney-client privilege and perhaps, and I know Mr. Haynes can defend this principle better than I can, but perhaps they should have a chance to discuss that whether or not they feel the need to object to it or not. I -- because for the record and for the future of this case, as we all know, no one gives up that right by taking the witness stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. You will not be surprised if I confess to you that this has been moving in all directions at the back of my mind all the time. However, I did not notice Mr. Haynes stand up and object.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was watching the clock as well. I thought we could get to 10.20 and I'd think about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take the break now then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Twenty-five minute break from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, have you had -- and Mr. Bourgon, have you had a chance to talk?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon says he has one more question on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we can proceed, I suppose. Mr. Bourgon, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I have one last question on this topic concerning your review of your -- of the evidence in this case before your testimony, and I'd simply like you to confirm that in preparing for your testimony before this Chamber, you did not ignore any evidence which was contrary to what you, today, say is the truth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that I and my defence team in preparing for the testimony went through the evidence already admitted. All I want to say is that I always had endless trust in professionalism and responsibility of members of my team, that they acknowledged my military profession, and I recognise their professional legal knowledge. And in the course of preparing the defence case, I provided all the information that I had available relating to my engagement and the events that are subject of this case. I don't know if this same thing applies to other Defence teams, we never gave it a thought actually. During preparations, we worked together and the lead counsel was in charge of the preparation in general, and I was there to explain to him anything that from a military point of view he couldn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be useful when we get to the events of 16 July. At this time, what I would like to do is to ask you, now that I have completed your examination-in-chief, and that you have heard all of the evidence in this case which was presented both by the Prosecution and by the -- your co-accused in this case, I would like to ask you if you believe, at least from the military point of view, you bear any responsibility for the crimes that were committed in the area of Zvornik in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expressed my opinion about the indictment almost three years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But that was before you heard all the evidence in this case. Now that you've heard all the evidence, and I'm not seeking a legal conclusion from you, I'm seeking a conclusion as the brigade commander, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade in July 1995; and I'm asking you straightforward: Do you believe you bear any responsibility from a military perspective for the events that took place there at the time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And looking back at these events, do you believe today as a military commander that you could have done something to save the lives of those Muslim prisoners who were executed during this period?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, those who were executed before I learned about that, it was impossible. Those who we captured remained alive as well as those who were allowed to pass through. Whoever -- whoever's life depended on me, they survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, you said that you were surprised when you learned that Obrenovic pled guilty. That was at page 31331, lines 7 to 8. And it's also my understanding that you said that you did not think that Obrenovic was guilty on the basis of the information he communicated to you in 1995, and that was at page 31333, line 24, to 31335, line 2. Do you maintain this view today?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my question is the following, I'd like to review some facts and then put a similar question to you: On the basis of your testimony, you will agree with me that Obrenovic obtained information about executions in Orahovac at the latest in the evening of 14 July during his conversation with Jokic, who was the brigade operations duty officer. That was your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it's your testimony that you arrived at the Zvornik Brigade command at around mid-day on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it was your testimony that in the afternoon of 15 July, you were informed that prisoners were being held in schools in the Zvornik area including Petkovci and Pilica?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it's your testimony that Obrenovic kept this information until he conveyed it to you on the 16th of July at around 6.00?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 1800 hours, you're right. And you know on the basis of all the evidence that we've heard in this case, that during this time, a large number of prisoners who were held in Pilica and Petkovci schools were executed. You're familiar with this evidence?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on the basis of these facts, is it still your position that from a military perspective, you bear no responsibility for these executions which took place in those schools?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you believe that the fact that the place of execution and the place where prisoners of war were kept, held captive was in the area of Zvornik where the Zvornik Brigade was the -- makes the brigade responsible for that, then I don't think you're right. It was someone else who did this business, organised everything and executed everything. Had it by any chance happened that they had taken these prisoners to another location, and that they had met the same fate, I never would have been here, nor would anyone ask any questions of the Zvornik Brigade about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me make my question more precise. Dragan Obrenovic was your subordinate, and for two days he had information about executions taking place in Orahovac, and you had both the means to find out this information and the duty to find out this information; and this information included the participation of elements of the Zvornik Brigade. Do you believe that you have no responsibility whatsoever for those events?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Dragan Obrenovic conveyed this information to me and also later, there was no information or report about the participation of members of the Zvornik Brigade in the events. If Obrenovic was responsible and had any role in the events of the 14th and the morning of the 15th, then the corps command who was his superior command at the time should have requested him to provide this information or undertake certain measures against him. The command didn't do anything which is one of the indicators based on which I believe that Obrenovic was not responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on the basis of this answer, Mr. Pandurevic, what I'd like to do at this time, and that's my purpose, is to try and understand your point of view from the military perspective so I can better understand how it is that you testified the way you did concerning Drago Nikolic. During your examination-in-chief, when you testified about the conversation you had with Obrenovic in your office concerning the executions on -- that was the conversation of 23 July -- you stated and I quote from page 31171, lines 11 to 12: "But according to the information that we had, we knew that the order had come from General Mladic." Do you recall testifying to that effect?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And later, on the same page or on page 31172, lines 7 to 9, you said: "However in light of the subsequent events, and the fact that no measures were taken, I'm still convinced that the order did, indeed, come from him." Do you stand by this testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At page 31106, you also testified as follows. And I quote: "On the 18th of July, when you dictated this report" -- that was the question, sorry. "Q. On the 18th of July when you dictated this report, did you have any reason to believe, for example, that General Krstic knew anything about the killing operation of the prisoners?" The answer was: "I did not have any kind of explicit information that would point to the fact that General Krstic knew something about that. However, I was thinking logically since he had not reacted to my report sent on the 15th, since in the course of the conversation that we conducted in the morning of the 17th, since never happened after my report on the 16th, I fully believe that he was in possession of certain information." Do you remember testifying to that effect?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at page 31112, you also testified that when talking about the sources of your information about crimes committed, and again I quote you, lines 19 to 23: "The main source of my information was Dragan Obrenovic, and on the 18th in Baljkovica, Jokic confirmed to me the engagement of the engineering machinery and one machine from the Birac Holding enterprise and one machine from the stone quarry from Josanica." Do you recall testifying to that effect?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you will also agree with me that in your examination-in-chief, talking about reburials, you expressed the view and I quote 31244, lines 13 to 18: "I did not have any direct information about who was engaged in this, who was in charge of it, but I was able to conclude that it was being done by the security organs because no task had been issued to any of the commands for them to pass the orders down the chain of command and deal with this matter." Do you recall testifying to that effect?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I could continue with more examples from your examination-in-chief, but my question is the following: Bearing in mind your testimony in this case, help me out in understanding if I am right in saying that according to you, the chain of command from the Main Staff to the corps, the security organs of the VRS, Mladic, Krstic, Jokic, were involved and are responsible to some degree for the crimes that are committed against prisoners of war in the Zvornik area in 1995, but that you, Mr. Pandurevic, have no responsibility whatsoever. Is that what we are to understand from your ten days of testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will understand it in the way you can and want to understand it. I had no command responsibility or personal responsibility for those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's try and explore a bit further into this. I'm not saying that I want to have an understanding, I'm saying this is my understanding. Am I right or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That's for the Trial Chamber to decide, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move to a different topic of my cross-examination dealing with forcible transfer. If I can have in e-court, please, P5. Sir, you will recognise this document -- sorry, it's not there yet. That's P5. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Be patient, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's a long document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have the Tribunal logo at the moment. Do you want to go to any particular page?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, the first page will be fine for now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine. If you look at your monitor, Mr. Bourgon, you will see that the English version that we have does not correspond with the -- okay, it does now. Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you recognise this document which appears before you on the screen as being the directive for upcoming operations to the command of the 1st -- addressed to the command of the 1st -- sorry, it's the directive for further operations number 7. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have seen it in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now you see the date of this document is 8 March 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But if we go back one page at least on the English side, we see the cover letter, which is page 1 in e-court on the English side. So we see from this page that this is a document that came from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and that it was addressed to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps by Milovanovic, the Chief of Staff, on 17 March. Do you recognise this cover letter, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it here for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly my point leading into my next question. During your examination-in-chief, and that was on page 30821, lines 21 to 24, you said that you saw this document for the first time here in The Hague; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that this is a strategic level document?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you will also agree with me that if you did not see it until you arrive in The Hague, nobody else in the Zvornik Brigade did; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that you would not expect brigade officers in general to be informed of strategic level documents issued by the Supreme Command of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to another document which is P203 in e-court, please. We have this document now on the screen, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Bourgon. Just out of curiosity, even though out of the back of my mind I seem to remember something, can you -- okay. I notice, although I do remember that there was an explanation for this, that while the B/C/S version at the top right-hand corner says copy number 6 P, in the English, it says copy number 9. I just want a confirmation, nothing else, that we're talking exactly of the same document. Later on the title does seem to indicate that we're talking about operative order number 7. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we'll check on that. I believe this will -- I believe it's been in evidence that this Directive 7 was sent around to the different brigades. We may have translated one that came from a different brigade but we'll check on that. It shouldn't change the substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I seem to remember that this was brought up earlier on in the course of the trial but I just wanted to -- in case you need or you wish to make any submission regarding this. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's also not on the list of documents that has been disclosed, P203 but I have no objection at this stage. I may have something to say about that a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise to my colleague. I thought -- we thought this document was on our list, and I will take this at the break but it's a document that is of -- very well known that was used in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. No, that I know. But let's proceed then, and I will reserve your respective rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I thank you, Mr. President, for raising the issue about the copy number 9 and number 6 in the B/C/S version, and I will also follow-up on this with my colleagues from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then there is one in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, you see that this is -- this document is called "Order For Defence and Active Combat Operations, Operative No. 7." You've seen this document during your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can move to page 6 in English and page 3 in B/C/S, please. Now, sir, if we look in item number 2, and I think this one appears in the middle of the page in your language and in English, I'm looking at the last sentence of the first paragraph where it says or the infamous sentence appears: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Sir, it was your testimony that this sentence was copy pasted word for word from the strategic document that we looked at, the directive for further operations 7, which you never saw during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only this sentence, but the task given to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well I move now to the tasks and the order which was -- which is issued by this document. If I can go to page 8 in English and page 4 in B/C/S. Now, under item 4, under the heading, "I have decided," we see that there is no reference whatsoever to that infamous phrase including in item 2 about the survival of the inhabitants of Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on the basis of your military experience, you can say that what matters in an order of this type is the decision of the corps commander which is expressed in this paragraph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From point 4 to the end of the order, all that is considered to be a decision in the military sense. The first part is the idea behind it, and it's important for the subordinate command receiving this order in studying its task because it has to understand the goal and the idea of the superior commander who issued the order; so the part containing the idea behind the decision reached by General Zivanovic is to separate the two enclaves and prevent communication between them and nothing more than that as regards the enclaves themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as far as you were concerned as the commander of the Zvornik Brigade receiving this document, what is important for you is the decision part from paragraphs 4 and onwards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can move to page 9 in English and page 5 in B/C/S. This section, sir, under item 5, "The tasks of the units," we see at paragraph 5.1, that these are the tasks which were assigned to the Zvornik Brigade by this order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I'd like to cover two specific parts of paragraph 5.1, namely the first part which starts after the colon with a little dash, and it says that your task or that of the Zvornik Brigade was to: "Prevent an enemy breakthrough along selected tactical axes, taking control of dominant features, cutting the Zvornik-Kozluk road and reaching the Drina River." Was that the main task that you were assigned as commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the main task throughout the war. So it didn't have to be written down specially, everybody knew about it, and it was only being reiterated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In other words, concentrate on the forward defence line and prevent a breakthrough from the Muslim 2nd Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the main rationale for the existence of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the last task in this paragraph 5.1, which is the third little dash which says: "The brigade command shall form battalion-strength ready forces for the intervention along threatened axes and carrying out offensive operations in their area of responsibility and by the order of the Drina Corps commander." Can you explain to us what this means?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is practically reiterating a task we had been given previously. This battalion had been established, and that was the Podrinje Detachment of special forces with reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the purpose of this task is to have forces ready to intervene both in your area of responsibility and, of course, if the Drina Corps commander needs some assistance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But as you mentioned in your examination-in-chief, there is no mention whatsoever in this paragraph 5.1 of either Srebrenica enclave or Zepa enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your examination-in-chief, you stated at 30829, lines 6 to 16, the question was: "Q. Now going back to, as it were, the infamous words which are set out under paragraph 2, the tasks of the Drina Corps, how did you or do you view the task of the Drina Corps under that heading in terms of achievability?" Your answer was: "When I received this order, I first read it and we call it the first reading, just to get the general idea. During that first reading, I noticed item 2, the task of the corps. However, I did not dwell long on it and during the next reading and analysing, I focused on item 4. I cannot tell you now exactly what I understood at the time. The sentence has been mentioned here, but definitely I gave it a lot of thought in this trial." So my understanding on the basis of this answer, Mr. Pandurevic, is that when you read this order coming from the corps and that you acted upon it in accordance with your duties as brigade commander, you focused exclusively on the commander's decision-making and the tasks issued to the Zvornik Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
