utterances.text: Yes, and the neighbouring brigades. That was the Sekovici Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And we've heard lots of evidence in this case, sir, about the staffing process which follows once you receive such an order from the corps; and you will agree with me that the staffing process, of course, is directed by both you and your Chief of Staff inside the Zvornik Brigade command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The process was started by the commander and then continued by the Chief of Staff and the other staff organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that during the complete staffing process which followed receiving this order, that which took place within the Zvornik Brigade command, you never discussed, indicated in any way, nor made any request to your Chief of Staff, your assistant commanders, and your staff officers in relation to actions targeted at the civilian population of Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was absolutely not to be considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if I put myself today or -- no, not today, but then in the shoes of any of these officers, whether your Chief of Staff, your assistant commanders, or your staff officers in the command, would you agree with me that I could not infer from your orders and instructions as brigade commander that the Zvornik Brigade had anything to do or any actions to do in the sense of targeting the civilian population of Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your conclusion is correct. The order I issued based on this order starts with point 1 where I put forward information on the enemy in front of the brigade zone. Point 2 would be the brigade's tasks, the one contained in this order issued by the corps commander. Point 3 would be the task of the neighbouring brigade, the Sekovici Brigade; and point 4 would be my idea behind the decision for the engagement of the brigade in the spirit of the assigned task and nowhere would Srebrenica or Zepa be mentioned in all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one last question on this topic, and you covered this at length during your examination-in-chief. It is your testimony that the Zvornik Brigade, to your knowledge, was never involved in any way in the forcible transfer of the civilian population from Potocari to Kladanj in Muslim-held territory?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the same applies for the civilian population of Zepa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a different part of my cross-examination and in this part I would like to go back to your testimony in relation to the period from 12 to 15 July 1995, that is before you left the area of Zepa to return to Zvornik. The first issue I would like to address is the command relationship between Major Obrenovic and yourself during this period. Based on your testimony, it is my understanding that according to you, from the moment you left Zvornik with Tactical Group 1, Major Obrenovic was acting in his capacity as deputy commander of the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He was the acting brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you had no responsibility, according to your testimony, whatsoever, for anything that happened until you resumed your functions as commander; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was prevented from carrying out the duties of the commander of the Zvornik Brigade in that period because I was carrying out another task, and in that period, there was no command relationship, no superior-subordinate relationship between Dragan Obrenovic and me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we'll move to the -- your arrival in the Zvornik Brigade command on 15 July a little later, but my question is when exactly do you resume in your functions as commander? What's the exact defining moment when Major Obrenovic no longer was the acting brigade commander and that you resume your functions?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he completed the briefing in his office, I think that I then said, Now I'm taking over the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what you are basically saying is once you are -- once you have been informed or you got the briefing as to the situation in which the brigade is, then it's for you to decide whether you resume command or not; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Krstic was the one who sent me back and I had to assume command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What if someone would say that the moment General Krstic gave you the order to go back, you were now the brigade commander. What would you say to such an allegation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That allegation would be illogical and untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Help us in understanding why.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because actually it produced no effect on the spot and by that, I mean in the brigade zone. Because I was still not there, I was still not able to command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you spoke on the phone that morning with Jokic, Milosevic, and Mijatovic, were they speaking to the commander of the brigade or were they speaking to someone who was yet to resume his functions as commander?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think that they tried to contact Obrenovic, but I think they failed to do so because he was in the field; and, therefore, they spoke to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe my question is not precise enough. Those calls were initiated by you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you speak to these three individuals as we've seen from the intercepts, are you speaking as the person who has resumed his command over the Zvornik Brigade or are you still not yet commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was commander formally speaking, but I didn't resume my duties as commander of the brigade yet. Let me give you another example. When I set off from Visegrad to assume duties of the Zvornik Brigade command, I didn't become the brigade commander automatically in Visegrad. It happened only when I arrived in Zvornik, received all the information necessary, and sat at the command -- brigade commander's desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I agree with what you're saying about the moving from the Visegrad Brigade to the Zvornik Brigade but you will agree with me that beforehand you had no relationship whatsoever with the Zvornik Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in the instance that we're talking about, you were, before leaving with Tactical Group 1 and during your deployment with Tactical Group 1 formally still the commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you spoke on the phone that morning to those three individuals I've mentioned, could you issue them orders, for example?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have issued orders but I didn't do so because I was not in command of the brigade. That would amount to dual command, not single authority because Dragan Obrenovic had already issued them tasks, and they were in the process of carrying out and that would only create confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So that was an understanding, or is it your understanding that both you and those three individuals understood that on that moment within you spoke to them, and you were asking for information about the 4th and the 7th Battalion, that you were not speaking to them as the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I received this information in order to discuss with Krstic the request for my being sent back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I understand you correctly, based on what you're saying now is that once you left with Tactical Group 1, you no longer cared what happened at the Zvornik Brigade because there was an officer there, Obrenovic, who was qualified to talk over and you did not need to worry about what was going on there; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have to be concerned, and I couldn't make any decisions and I couldn't influence the operation of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But as you've mentioned, formally you were still the brigade commander because Obrenovic did not get a formal appointment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An individual who is prevented from carrying out their duties is given a standee because according to establishment of president of the Chief of Staff is at the same time the deputy commander, and the rule on the regiment command says that in absence of the commander, the Chief of Staff stand in for the commander with all his respective duties and responsibilities. Therefore, Obrenovic was in command of the brigade. The individual who is absent is formally registered as being in this post, but there could be a variety of reasons for this individual not to be able to carry out his duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I think we are very close to each other on this, but my question is simply once you -- still being the formal commander of the brigade, do you forget about that brigade or you still have military responsibilities towards that brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have command responsibility, but I cannot disregard the brigade, and my command post cannot be outside the brigade zone because the communications lines that I use in commanding are within my zone and have certain range. My forward command post cannot be in Zepa while I command the brigade in Zvornik, for example. Even if I had such a large connection that wouldn't have given me the right to command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So then, sir, I take it that you will agree with me that during this period, we're talking specifically 12 to 15 July, but I could extend that period, that even though from a legal point of view you may not bear any responsibilities for crimes committed in your absence, now that's a legal question and is not something I wish to address at this time, you'll agree with me that from a military perspective you were still formally the commander and you still had a duty of care for your brigade. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I didn't have the duty to care because I was prevented from carrying out my duties. What I thought was just my choice, and I could have thought anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I suggest to you, sir, that when you obtained information of the threat posed by the column and the 28th Division moving towards the area of Zvornik that was sufficient reason for you to be informed -- not to be informed, sorry, it was sufficient information for you to take some actions to at least find out what was happening in Zvornik at the time.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information served only for me to send a request to General Krstic to eliminate the reasons for my being prevented from commanding the Zvornik Brigade. At 9.00 on the 15th, I was commanding the TG at the IKM at Krivace which was in combat engagement with the enemy. That was my basic task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I will be straightforward with my case here. I'm putting to you here that during this period when you were away, that you did remain in contact with Major Obrenovic contrary to your testimony in this case, and I'd like to cover that aspect step by step. Firstly you mentioned during your examination-in-chief and that was at 30741 lines 15 to 20: "That it is not right for the commander of a brigade to be called upon to participate in combat activities outside of the area of operations of his own brigade." You added: "This does not or should not happen in organised armies." Do you still agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Nonetheless, when you received the order for Krivaja 95 and that is asking for Tactical Group 1 to be put together and to take part in combat activities near Srebrenica, you did not hesitate in assigning yourself as commander of Tactical Group 1, which means I suggest to you that you accepted to deprive the Zvornik Brigade of its commander for the time that you would be away in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is contrary to the laws of physics, Mr. Bourgon. I didn't assign myself. It was an order from Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well I suggest to you, and we can go to the order if you want, but that this order never said that you were to take command of this Tactical Group 1, or that you were to create Tactical Group 1; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it was your choice to take command of this tactical group?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my choice, because this tactical group was twice as strong than the forces given by the 1st Romanija or the 1st Birac brigades. Each one of them gave a company, it was not reasonable for a brigade commander to command a company. The Zvornik Brigade provided a reinforced light infantry battalion, it is quite understandable in view of the task received for me to assume command of this unit because it was made up of three different units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that it was understandable that you, nonetheless, decided to do so; but that was not part of the order, was it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an oral order from General Krstic for me to command these forces from the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, we've seen the order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Bourgon, let me intervene here. Had you, Mr. Pandurevic, instead of taking -- assuming the command of this tactical group appointed, say, Obrenovic, to take command of it, what would have been the consequences, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would have stayed at the brigade command and commanded the Zvornik Brigade. Only this part of the tactical group would not be under my command but under Obrenovic's command or rather General Krstic's command. Because Obrenovic didn't have any responsibility towards TG-1 which was under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So Mr. Pandurevic, all I'm saying is that you could have appointed, instead of yourself, for example, Legenda or Bojanovic or Strbac to take command of that group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree about Legenda as the person capable of commanding, but the other two names are an unfortunate choice. They couldn't have done this duty. I could have appointed anyone but what would that mean? That would be really irresponsible. I wouldn't carry out the task of the core. I had an oral order from the corps commander to command these forces personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now just for the record would you agree with me that this is the first time that this oral order from General Krstic is ever mentioned this trial? Do you agree with me on this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I mentioned Krstic's order before. Whether I specified that it was an oral one, I don't think it makes any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It was simply an oversight on your part.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like -- when you created Tactical Group 1 and you took command of the group, I take it you were aware that once you were away with this Tactical Group, the brigade would be short or deprived of very important resources to hold the line facing the 2nd Corps of the Muslim army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These resources would not be lacking because in the period, the number of soldiers on defence line increased in this period. They were called off from their leave, and they were deployed in positions. The Podrinje Detachment of special forces never held any positions on defence line. The Zvornik Brigade had sufficient strength to defend from any possible attack by the 2nd Corps. The estimate of the Drina Corps commander was such that they needed those forces and given the Muslim operation offensive around Sarajevo, we knew that their intervention forces from the 2nd Corps had been sent to the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I could just make just one question. Was there a reference to General Krstic as the commander of the corps at this point? Is that a translation issue or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon. Which part of the transcript are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: One example, Mr. President, is at page 55, lines 19 and line 14 also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was the General's answer that I was questioning, whether or not the translation was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pandurevic, can you help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 55, line 14.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I understand Mr. McCloskey's interventions. General Krstic was, at the time, still the Chief of Staff and the deputy commander of the corps, but he was in command of Krivaja 95 operation and a limited number of the forces from the Drina Corps were involved in that operation. General Ivanovic [as interpreted] was totally side tracked at the time but he certainly had a approval from Zivanovic for me to go there and command my forces taking part in Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Mr. Pandurevic. You can proceed, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to have in e-court, please, P318. I believe this one is on our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, is it your position that when you left with Tactical Group 1, pursuant to the orders that you had received, according to your testimony, that this had no impact or no effect on the Zvornik Brigade or what was left of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all related as a cause and consequence. I'm not viewing things in isolation. I'm viewing them as a whole. If I left the brigade zone of defence and the deputy commander stayed back to command the brigade which was confirmed several times in various documents, the Zvornik Brigade was not hampered by that. It remained with enough manpower and capable of carrying out the task given to them. At that point, nobody thought that some day, the 28th Division would find itself in the defence zone of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So leaving aside for now the fact that the 28th Division did appear in Zvornik, it's your position that the brigade was perfectly able to cope with its duties and tasks while you were away with Tactical Group 1; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the tasks that it had been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the document, which is on the screen before you, do you recognise this as being your order highlighting or stating the composition of Tactical Group 1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise this, and everything that is written here is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if we move to page 2 of this document, we have -- so at paragraph 2.2, sir, we see that the first battle group was composed of the Podrinje Detachment and we see at the letters E for Echo as part of this battle group, you included the 82-millimetre Mortar Platoon. Was that a unit formally attached to the Podrinje Detachment or did that come from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was part of the Podrinje Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at letters G for Golf, the Zolja Intervention Platoon from the 4th Battalion, this intervention platoon was composed of the best fighters from the 4th Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the detachment was incomplete, and it was almost 100 men short than usual because part of their forces were in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I look at the composition of the second battle group at paragraphs 2.3, we see that all of these resources are resources that were taken away from the Zvornik Brigade when you left for Tactical Group 1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we see the two companies have been formed within this combat group made up of three platoons each; each platoon had about 20 soldiers, each company had -- which is twice the smaller number than the usual, and these were men from the Zvornik Brigade. Had they not joined the tactical group, they would have been on leave. They wouldn't be on the positions of the Zvornik Brigade. Maybe not these particular men but some others, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I look at paragraphs 2.4 where is it says, "The Armoured Mechanised Company," those four T-55 tanks, they were no longer with the Zvornik Brigade when you left, you took them with you.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. They were part of the detachment per establishment, but I reshuffled the detachment and other battalions and units and I set up a special support unit of this tank company, however, some other tanks, T-34, for example, remained in the zone brigade which were fortified firing positions and were excellent for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we move to the next page on the English side and also next page on the B/C/S side, and I refer you to also in paragraph 2.4, you see here the resources that you took with you, the 4 armoured personnel carriers, that's paragraph Bravo; the Praga with crew, that's paragraph Charlie; and the hand-held anti-aircraft rocket, the Strela 2m at paragraph Bravo. And we also see that at 2.5, there is a platoon of 122 millimetres. Were all of these resources that were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Previous page on B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In the previous page -- these were all resources that were taken away from the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that is listed here has been taken away from the Zvornik Brigade. We do not have to go item by item. These armoured transporters and the Praga were always going with the Podrinje Detachment if it was operating outside the brigade zone with the exception of 122 howitzers which were taken from the mixed artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well then leaving that list aside would you agree with me, sir, that when you left with Tactical Group 1, you took the best fighters of the brigade with you leaving behind people with little or no combat experience to hold the line; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had equal combat experience as the soldiers in TG-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Tactical Group 2, I'm talking about those left in Zvornik to hold the line. The people left in Zvornik, I suggest to you, were people with little or no combat experience; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, Mr. Bourgon. I've been saying the same thing but as regards experience, the experience of the soldiers who remained to defend the brigade zone is the same as the experience of the men in Combat Group 2 who left with me. They were all mobilised at the same time, and they had spent the same amount of time waging war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, based on the information that you had at the time, I take it that when you left with Tactical Group 1, and you referred to that earlier, you did not expect the Zvornik Brigade to face any major situation or to be involved in any type of heavy fighting when you were away; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. If someone had listened to me at the meeting in Bratunac on the 11th, they would not have had to face that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you trusted when you went away with Tactical Group 1 that Obrenovic could fulfill the duties of deputy commander because he had done so in the past; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But it could not be expected, at least at the time, that a column of many thousands of Muslims would soon be crossing the area of operations of the Zvornik Brigade trying to breach your line of defence and reach Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could not be expected to happen that way. I did entertain some assumptions, but it was only on the 12th that we learned of the specific intentions of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I am interested in, sir, is that what you did, once you realised that the 28th Division was heading for Zvornik, there was a possibility at the time, would you agree with me, that the 28th Division would even capture Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there was no possibility of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did the column and the 28th Division represent a major threat for Zvornik and the Zvornik Brigade or what was left of it at the time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 12th of July onwards, the Army of Republika Srpska had specific information about the axis of movement and the intentions of the 28th Division. That column had only one goal and that was to reach the territory of the 2nd Corps by the shortest route or the route they knew best, in the fastest way, and with the least obstruction. They had previously reconnoitred those axes for that column to aside to attack Zvornik would have been crazy and those commanders in the units of the 28th Division never even thought of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, you had fought a part of the 28th Division just a few hours before that. Would you agree with me that you were aware of the determination and the fire power which could be mustered by the 28th Division if it reached the territory of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obrenovic himself knew on the 12th, he had information about the movements of the 28th Division. On the 13th and 14th, his information was complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But my question is what did you have as information at the time concerning the threat posed by the 28th Division to Zvornik, and what did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody sent me any information, nor did I, after leaving Vijogor going towards Zepa, inquire about it. My last contact at Vijogor with Krstic and Mladic was when I learned from them that there was sufficient and adequate forces to stop any further movement of the 28th Division, and I didn't worry about it anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We'll cover your encounter with Krstic and Mladic, but before you had this encounter were you worried at any time concerning the threat posed by the 28th Division to the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put forward my thoughts and my suggestions at the meeting of the 11th. They were rejected. They were not accepted. After that, I could think whatever I wanted, but I could no longer influence the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you find the need at any point in time to contact Major Obrenovic to inform him of the threat and at least find out what he was doing or what he was planning to defend against this threat?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't contact him at all. He was on the radio network with the corps command. The corps and Dragan Obrenovic had much more information about the 28th Division than I did; in fact, I had no information at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what you're saying today that Major Obrenovic was on the radio network with the corps and that he had all the information, the same information that General Krstic possessed at the time; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had the same information as Krstic, but we saw here from a number of documents what activities Obrenovic undertook with respect to the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, how big was the 28th Division? What was your knowledge of the size of the 28th Division at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get a specific date? It's sort of disappearing rather quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Between the 12 and the 15 of July when you realised that there is a column including the 28th Division moving towards Zvornik, what was your understanding of the size of that force moving towards Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information about the approximate numbers of the 28th Division which was in Srebrenica on the 11th. When the VRS entered Srebrenica and the 28th Division pulled out in the direction the Jaglici, we had assessments to the effect that part of the division would try to break through towards Zepa, one part towards Kladanj, and one part towards Tuzla through the Zvornik area; but we did not know the numbers of the forces who would be trying to break through in each of those axes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What was your information that you possessed at the time concerning the total numbers in the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Exactly at that period. What was the total number of the 28th Division by the time you lounged or you set out with Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information that there were about 6.000 members of the 28th Division in the Srebrenica area holding positions at the approaches to Srebrenica. When that number started pulling out, they were divided in different directions, but how many of them were in each of those directions, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I don't think you answered my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time it's convenient for you, Mr. Bourgon, we'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I think that's a convenient time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon, and please leave about five, maximum 10 minutes towards the end because I understand Mr. Haynes would like to raise an issue. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think five will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay, then five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, just before the break, I wanted to go back to a question, which I felt you did not answer, and the question was that I suggest to you that you were fully aware of the determination of the members of the 28th Division and their will to fight and to reach Tuzla by all means. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't fully aware of that because I did not have a clear picture of their evil intentions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or rather of all their intentions, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that they wanted to reach the area of the 2nd Corps going through several -- taking several routes not in a single column.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But my question relates to the fact that you had been fighting them for some days by that time. Were they good fighters or were they determined fighters?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were very persistent along my axis of attack because they were fortified, they had well-dug trenches and shelters, parapets. And I think they had more reason to fight then than later on when they lost those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I take it that you are familiar with the weapons which the 28th Division had in its possession?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the weapons they used along my axis of attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But were you aware that the 28th Division was a well-armed division?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was well-armed with a light-automatic, and semi-automatic weapons, a certain number of mortars of 82 millimetres, anti-aircraft machine-guns of 12.7 millimetres, a 20-millimetre gun, and I found a B-176-millimetre gun as well and some hand-held launchers and other anti-armour equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me share with you, sir, some of the figures that were given in the Krstic trial by General Hadzihasanovic, who was the Chief of Staff of the ABiH as you know. He gave some figures in his testimony about the weapons in the possession of the 28th Division and that was on 5 April 2001, page 9517. These figures include according to him, 1.947 automatic rifles; 13 sniper rifles; 27 submachine-guns; 15 machine-guns; 12, 60-millimetre mortars; five 82-millimetre mortars; nine hand-grenade launchers; four recoilless guns, 82-millimetre; 68-hand held rocket launchers, zolja type; one light rocket launcher of Fagot type, the 9K11F, which you are familiar with; and four anti-aircraft guns of 20 millimetres. Is that the arsenal that you were familiar with that could be in the possession of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are more or less the weapons I enumerated by kind and purpose. The information given here is precise, whether it's correct or not, I'm not sure but after withdrawal of the 28th Division during the breakthrough, only the automatic weapons and the light machine-guns could be used. The other weapons could not be carried apart from the hand-held launchers which are carried on the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I take it you will agree with me that coming from an officer from the Muslim army, that this is most likely a very conservative estimate as to all the weapons which were in the possession of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can only say the following: That the Muslim command or rather the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina claimed, after the demilitarisation, that they had no weapons and here, we see the figure of 2.000. I have no reason to doubt the figures provided here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you are also aware, sir, on the basis of your experience that many people from the 28th Division were also using personal rifles such as hunting rifles, for example?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read that in various statements, and I heard some people testify to that here. There were quite a few hunters in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, it's your testimony that -- just to come back on one quick point concerning the fact that the Zvornik Brigade was not shorthanded at the time, would you agree with me that this column moving towards the Zvornik territory was a major threat for the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we bear in mind the principles for the tactical use of units breaking through from encirclement is a specific kind of combat activity. It is always undertaken in order to break through in the direction of the nearest forces belonging to the same side and these were first in Zepa then in Kladanj and only then in Nezuk. The column, however, decided to take the longest route and to march as a single column. This was a military target and a military threat, but how far it was fit for combat after 6 or 7 days' march, that's another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the fact that the column would appear in the Zvornik territory, therefore, taking the Zvornik Brigade in kind of a sandwich between the 2nd Corps and the column, this was an unprecedented situation for the Zvornik Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the first instance where the Zvornik Brigade was facing conflict both from the front and from the rear to this extent. There had been previous attempts to break out from the Konjevic Polje and Cerska area via Crni Vrh, but these were units of up to about 500 fighters, so the Zvornik Brigade had not faced this kind of situation before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, knowing that this threat was on the way towards the Zvornik Brigade, it is not testimony that not once did you call or try to call Major Obrenovic to warn him and to discuss with him the situation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have any contact with Mr. Obrenovic at that time, nor did I tell him of the threat emanating from the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you agree that it was possible for you to contact the Zvornik Brigade by using any civilian phone in the area where you were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have the technical capability to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your testimony, you mentioned two occasions on which you called back the brigade, on the 5th of July to get additional tank ammunition, that was on page 30892; and then on 7 July, when you called the duty officer because you remembered some teaching materials that had to be photo copied and delivered to the students of the school. That was at 30919. So you maintain your testimony that those are the only two instances where you called back the Zvornik Brigade when you were away with Tactical Group 1.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my recollection, those were the two instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, these, as you know, you will confirm that those are the only two instances which are recorded in the brigade duty officers' notebook. You didn't see any other instances in the brigade duty officers' notebook?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no other instances were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that if you had called or if you did call Dragan Obrenovic in his office, this would not be written in the duty officers' notebook; in fact, we've seen many intercepts of conversations involving members of the Zvornik Brigade command which were not written in the duty officers' notebook. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably there were such conversations, but it was my practice whenever I called the Zvornik Brigade outside the brigade area of defence, I always called the operations duty officer because I knew he would always be there. I would never know whether the Chief of Staff was in his office or not. So when I called from the IKM at Krivace, I called the operations duty officer, not Dragan Obrenovic on the 14th and the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What about, sir, the three cables that you told Eileen Gilleece that you received from the Chief of Staff Obrenovic during this period; did you receive any such cables during this period?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I received three telegrams from Chief Obrenovic but rather that three documents arrived, and one of them was the interim combat report sent by Dragan Obrenovic, not to me but to the corps command; but a copy arrived at the forward command post where Mr. Krstic was. The other documents concerned the radio reconnaissance platoon of the Drina Corps, and I think there was one document coming from Colonel Jocic. There may have been other documents as well, but I don't recall that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what you are saying now is that there was nothing important enough for you to call back your brigade even though you were, as you testified, worried about the column heading towards Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th, in the morning, I was given the task of launching an attack in the -- on the axis of Podzeplje-Brloska Planina and towards Zepa. That was a task issued to me by General Krstic. I was totally focused on that task. I wasn't worrying about the situation in the Zvornik Brigade because Dragan Obrenovic and the corps command were in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, if I look at the same situation from the point of view

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, on 10 February you testified about the period when you commanded the Drina Corps Brigade in the Krajina, and you stated and I quote from page 31203, lines 16 to 20: "I did call in several times in order to report if there were any losses, what the situation was among the men, so that the families of the fighters would have the information because they were concerned and there were rumours circulating about all the different events in the Krajina." So on the basis of this, your testimony, I suggest to you that it is not true that you were not in contact for the same purpose as a minimum with the Zvornik Brigade or with your Chief of Staff when you were away with Tactical Group 1.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert quite the opposite. These were two quite different situations. I think when I was referring to the material for the university, I said that we were working and that we were well. This material from the Krajina confirms that I was taking care of my men, and I was informing their families on whether there were any casualties, any men wounded, or killed, but this did not have any command purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you were away with Tactical Group 1, you also had some casualties but did not feel the need to call back and report on the situation of your men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Look at the report of the 10th, the daily combat report, and you will see that the names of the soldiers killed in Srebrenica are listed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how was this information -- how did that information make its way into the combat report of the 10th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the person who was in charge of this in the command of the tactical group sent this information through the corps forward command post because this information on losses is very important. If it's not timely and precise, various rumours start spreading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you send any reports through the forward command post of the corps while you were away with Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I reported to General Krstic on losses, on those killed and wounded in the course of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, coming back on the command relationship, you testified on 28 January, that was page 30760, that during the period you were away, the commander of Obrenovic was the corps commander. So in other words, Obrenovic was receiving his orders from the corps command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that he was the corps commander, but that he was directly subordinated to the corps commander, and he received orders from him and reported to him and send reports to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe you misunderstood or maybe it's not clear in the transcript, what I've mentioned is while you were away, the commander of Obrenovic was the corps commander. You said that; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So orders being issued to the Zvornik Brigade or to Obrenovic were issued by the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you would agree with me that during this period, nothing prevented either Major Obrenovic from contacting you to obtain advice or to inform you of the impossible situation he was placed in as deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he stood in for the commander, and his post or establishment was deputy. On the 14th, when he was in the most serious situation, he sent an interim report to the corps command requesting reinforcement. He didn't send this request to me nor did he ask me to come back. He had enough military training to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not saying that he sent that report to you. What I'm saying is that there is nothing preventing him from calling his formal commander from the situation he was in and to seek your advice as his formal commander, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was prevented by procedures and the military job because he knew that corps commander knew much more and had more information about what was going on in the corps zone than me who was engaged only on one axis within the zone and that I had limited information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So being placed in the most difficult of situations by two different -- for two different reasons, that is being informed of prisoners arriving in the zone of responsibility and being informed and not facing the column in his zone of responsibility, what you are saying is that you did not expect Major Obrenovic to call you at any time to inform you of this situation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not expect him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a different issue, and you said yesterday

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I have suggested to him to seek my opinion in this situation if I didn't know what the situation he was in. Secondly, the information that he had did not refer or had nothing to do with the Zvornik Brigade. It wasn't the Zvornik Brigade who was tasked with receiving and accommodating the prisoners. All they had was information that they were arriving, not to the barracks but rather that they would be placed in some non-military facilities. If I had been in the shoes of Major Obrenovic, I would have probably reasoned in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But if he had information that these prisoners were to be transported to the Zvornik area to be killed, then as you said yesterday, the least he could have done was to call the corps command and clarify the issue with them and undertake steps for such things not to occur; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is brought to my attention that we need some redaction at page 75, line 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's already been taken care of, Mr. Bourgon. Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And let's try to be a little more careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that when, and you've heard this evidence and we have the intercept to that effect that Major Obrenovic did speak, the night of 13 July with General Zivanovic, do you recall this intercept?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now during this conversation, he did not report to Major Obrenovic -- to General Zivanovic any information concerning the prisoners; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know if this conversation with General Zivanovic took place before he obtained that information or after. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: According to his statement of facts, this conversation took place after he obtained the information, but my question is the following: The fact that when he spoke to General Zivanovic, this was an open line or an un-secure line is not an excuse, you will agree with me, for not discussing the matter with his corps commander because there were other means that he could do that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that this could have been done in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my final question on this topic is the following: During your examination-in-chief, you said, and I quote: "If he," meaning Obrenovic, "had consulted you about whether he should give an order to have prisoners killed, what would you have said?" That was the question. The answer: "I would never have given him such an order." "Q. Well, this is really important. I'm going to try that again. If he had asked you about whether he should give such an order, what would you have said?" Your answer was: "I would have told him not to issue such an order at all." Do you recall saying this on 30 January?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It is my understanding, sir, that based on your answer, that if Obrenovic, one, would have had information about an order to kill prisoners of war on 13 July; and two, had he contacted you as I suggest to you he did on 13 July to inform you about such an order, you would have done everything in your power to stop those killings from taking place immediately upon being informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There are several questions in there and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is a compound question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think if the explicit suggestion is going to be made to General Pandurevic that he contacted Major Obrenovic on the 13th of July, it should be put in precise terms when, by what means, and what his information is as to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I note the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is definitely a compound question which was raised by Mr. Haynes, and I think it's a very valid one too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, if Obrenovic contacted you on the night -- had contacted you on the night of 13 July, and if he had information about an order to kill prisoners of war, you would have done everything in your power to stop the killings from taking place immediately upon being informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, I don't think that's actually any better. Is the suggestion going to be made that he did contact Obrenovic on the 13th or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think at this stage, Mr. Pandurevic has heard the question twice. I agree with you that the second question doesn't address the point raised by you directly or specifically, but I think it can be dealt with by Mr. Pandurevic now on his own. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This is a conditional question. First of all, there was no such conversation, and I had no such information. If I had received this kind of information, among other things, I would have instructed Obrenovic to contact the corps command, and I would have told him that under no circumstances should he issue such illegal orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very useful. That's the information I was looking at, and that question was favourable to you so I'm not understand the objections of my colleague. But I move to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During your testimony, you mentioned the fact that when you were sent back to Zvornik on the 15th of July in the morning, you possessed no information whatsoever concerning the fact that there were prisoners of war being taken in large numbers. Do you confirm this testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the next part of my cross-examination, I suggest, sir, that this is not true and that by the time you went back to Zvornik, you were informed of a large number of prisoners that had been taken by the Drina Corps and other units. And for this I will go through a number of steps. First of all, you can confirm that you did meet with Generals Krstic and Mladic on a number of occasions during the period from 12 to 15 July.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To try and make it as short as possible, on the 12th of July, you stated that you met in the morning in the sector of the Bojina repeater, that you were met there by Colonel Vicic, Colonel Andric, and General Krstic among others; do you recall testifying to that effect?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that at 1800 hours, the same day on the 12th July, you met again with Krstic in the area of Vijogor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at that time, General Krstic wanted to know whether there was any information that had been collected about elements of the 28th Division that were lagging behind?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he wanted to know whether we had come across elements of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's when for the first time you expressed your concerns to General Krstic about the column heading towards Zvornik. That was at page 30901, 30902; do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I only repeated my suggestion made at the meeting of the 11th vis-a-vis the 28th Division. I wanted to hear from General Krstic if he had any additional information about the intentions of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the morning of 13 July in the sector of the Bojina repeater, you were visited there by Krstic and Mladic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Not in the Bojina repeater sector but rather in Vijogor, and that was on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I refer to page 30905, but I will check that and move on just not to hold things up. On the 14th of July at 1000 hours while you were at the forward command post, you received the order Stupcanica and you reported to Krstic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And finally, to again just based on your testimony on 15 July, a few minutes before 900 hours in the morning, you had a meeting with Krstic at the forward command post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's where we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that on every one of these occasions, neither General Krstic nor General Mladic or any other officers at the forward command post of the corps informed you that a large number of prisoners had been captured and that they were or had been transferred to the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. They didn't inform me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you will agree, nonetheless, that during this period, both General Mladic and General Krstic would have been fully aware that a large number of prisoners had been captured along the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't have this information. During my examination-in-chief, I also said when was the first time that I assumed that it was possible for General Krstic to know about the prisoners of war in the area of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, for example, according to the adjudicated facts accepted by this Trial Chamber, I refer to fact number 271 and facts 278; 271 reads as follows: "Late in the afternoon of 13 July, General Mladic visited the meadow and told the men that they would not be hurt but would be exchanged as prisoners of war and that their families had been transported safely to Tuzla." Fact number 278: "General Mladic visited that field in the afternoon of 13 July as well." So you would agree that General Mladic would have been well aware of the prisoners at least as of 13 July.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is an adjudicated fact and as it is -- there is nothing for me to agree or not agree. I see that it happened in the afternoon, and I know that he met with me at Vijogor on the morning of the 14th [as interpreted]. Whether he knew about these men at the time, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now if we look at the position from General Krstic's point of view, one of the findings of the Trial Chamber in his trial was the following: "The Drina Corps command knew that thousands of Bosnian Muslim prisoners had been captured along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road on 13 July 1995." Now, in that case, the Trial Chamber referred to a number of documents which are also in evidence, so I'd like to look at two of these documents starting with 7DP1032 if I can have this document in e-court, please. I'll say the number again 7DP1032. So this document, Mr. Pandurevic, you will agree with me that it was from the command of the Drina Corps. It was on the 13th of July, and it was addressed to the forward command post of the Drina Corps as well as to all subordinated units and that it was dealing with preventing the passage of Muslim groups to Tuzla and Kladanj. I'm just reading from the document.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I refer to the second paragraph -- sorry, the first paragraph where at the end, it reads that, the last sentence: "There are hard-core criminals and felons among them who will go to any lengths to evade capture and reach the territory under Muslim control." Does that correspond with your understanding at the time of the determination of the members of the 28th Division trying to reach Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first saw this order here in this trial, this preamble contains the statements as you read them out, but I knew what actions had been taken by members of the 28th Division in fighting the Zvornik Brigade, and this knowledge that I have, have nothing to do with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'm not talking about your knowledge of the document, I'm saying if the contents of the documents corresponds to your knowledge at the time about the members of the division, their determination to reach territory under Muslim control. Does that correspond or what is there does not correspond? That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that members of the 28th Division had very serious intentions to break through towards the 2nd Corps at any costs, but I also know that they didn't have the strength to see that through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We'll cover whether they had the strength or not during my next part of my cross-examination but if I look at the next paragraph, Mr. Pandurevic, where it says: "During the night of the 12 and 13 July, part of these forces managed to escape and cross the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje-Milici-Vlasenica road and that they were observed heading towards Crni Vrh and Cerska." Would you agree with me on this basis what is written there that the command of the Drina Corps was very well aware as of the 12th of July, at least when this document was written, that the 28th Division had passed a critical point and was heading towards the area of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that this happened during the night between the 12th and the 13th. I don't know when this particular information was actually received, but one can see that they were cutting the road in two different sectors, one is Bratunac-Konjevic Polje, and this axis could lead towards Kamenica and Zvornik; and the other sector, Milici-Vlasenica and that is south-west, some 20 means which means that it can go towards Cerska and Kladanj; therefore, not all of them were headed towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's what it says, in part, if you look in the first paragraph where it says: "I hereby order, you see that the brigade commands in their area of responsibility are to employ all available, able-bodied men to discover, block, disarm, and capture any Muslim armed groups and prevent their crossing into Muslim territory." So there's no doubt about the intentions of the corps commander at that time, is there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you move to the next page, so we have paragraph 7 of this order and the next page in English too. We see at paragraph 7 that: "The order includes to transmit information on captured and cut-off groups through secure means of communication." Would you agree on the basis of this document that you would expect that if any subordinate units of the Drina Corps did capture prisoners, that the information would have been passed on to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here is that the information should be relayed through safe communication channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So would you expect the brigades to follow-up on this order and if they do capture members of the 28th Division, that they would report this to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but as far as we could see here, the Zvornik Brigade did not capture anyone until the 18th apart from some individuals on the 14th, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'm not referring to Zvornik Brigade at all. I'm talking subordinate units of the Drina Corps in general that they did -- that they would inform on the basis of this document, the corps command of any prisoners captured. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were supposed to report and this secrecy indicates that it was necessary to keep our intention secret and not divulged to the enemy including the deployment of our forces in order to make it easier for us to block them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have the next page of this document on the English side, please. You see at the bottom, sir, that the -- this document is dated the 13th of July and that it was signed at 1600 hours or 4.00 in the afternoon. I'm not sure if that's clear enough --

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it in the English version, but I can't see it in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have in e-court please document 4D81, 81.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, this document in front of you is a regular combat report. It was used with a number of witnesses in this case. I'd just like you to confirm, first of all, that it comes from the Drina Corps command and that it is addressed to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the daily combat report, the regular one, of the command of the Drina Corps dated the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And we see at the third paragraph under where it says, 1, "The enemy," the third paragraph, where it says that: "The enemy from the former Srebrenica enclave are in total disarray and have been surrendering to the VRS in great numbers."

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Lower down just above paragraph 4, paragraph 4 reads "unusual incidents. It says here: "In Konjevic Polje and also in Nova Kasaba, reception of Muslim civilians and soldiers who surrendered is being carried out, taken in an organised fashion." I don't think the next sentence has anything to do with that. Would you agree, sir, that on the basis of the information contained in this document that by the 13th of July, the Drina Corps command was fully aware that large numbers of prisoners were being made from that column heading towards Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on this report, I agree with that. This report also confirms that there was no concern as regards the security of Zvornik and the Zvornik Brigade's area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to the next page of this document in B/C/S, as well as page 3 in English. The information you just mentioned about no concerns for Zvornik, where did you see this, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the first part of the report, you said it said they were surrendering en masse and that 200 or 300 had managed to cross the road and get into the area of Udrc. Udrc is a mountain which was on the route towards Crni Vrh, which would mean to the corps command even had it wanted to couldn't have told me that the Zvornik Brigade was under threat. They knew only what was contained in this report; however, it transpired later that this information was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now if we look at paragraph 8 which is where I want to draw your attention, and the page 2 in B/C/S, sorry, where it says, paragraph 8: "Conclusions, projections, and decision for further action." "With regard to the situation created after the vigorous attack on the Srebrenica enclave and the successful pull-out of some of the extreme forces into the general sector" and that's what you were referring to a few moments ago, "and their intention of conducting further operations towards the Muslim-controlled territory ..." So would you agree with me that this report makes it clear that they know that at least part of those forces are heading towards Velja Glava, Krizevici and Baljkovica and that they have the intent to connect up with the forces which would operate from the Kladanj direction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an assessment. This is possible. The axes you mentioned are correct. In view of this conclusion, however, it's not clear to me why the Drina Corps failed to take proper steps later on to respond to this possible threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you see from this page also, at least on the English side, if I can have the next page in B/C/S that this combat report was by General Krstic and that the time was 1945 which is in the night of -- in the evening of 13 July.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my question is the following: Given that General Krstic is aware that prisoners are being captured in great numbers along the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje, as early as the evening of 13 July 1995, and bearing in mind your own testimony that he did not reply or did not take any actions in response to your interim combat report of 15 July, that General Krstic had the information concerning not only the taking of prisoners but where they had been sent. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this report of the 13th, which is before us, we see it doesn't say where those people were transferred and where they would be transferred to. It only says they were surrendering. I don't know whether Krstic knew where those people would go on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not saying he knew on the 13th, but it was your testimony that because he did not take action concerning your interim combat report of the 15th, that he was well aware of where the prisoners had been taken. Now, the only thing I'd like to find out from you before we end is that when you were returned to Zvornik on 15 July in the morning, I suggest to you that General Krstic would have informed you that there were prisoners, if he knew as you say, that there were prisoners that had been sent into your area and that before you left Zepa area, you knew about the prisoner problem before you arrived in Zvornik; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, Mr. Bourgon. My assessment, which I explained in my testimony based on the interim combat report of the 15th which followed on the evening was correct. Had General Krstic known something about it in Richard Butler's report we see an intercept on the morning around 10.00 where one of the participants was Krstic and prisoners are mentioned, so Krstic did know; but I did not have this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then I will leave it on one last question, Mr. Pandurevic. You testified in your examination-in-chief that General Krstic was aware of the situation involving the transfer of prisoners to Zvornik. Is it your testimony that he hid this information from you when he sent you back to defend the line and prevent the 28th Division from linking up the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a page and line reference for the assertion that General Pandurevic testified that General Krstic knew about the taking of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Should we leave it for Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I can put a line, Mr. President, but I'd like to have an answer to this question because this is something that I covered at the beginning of my cross-examination, and this is something that General said, and I refer to the page reference where he said exactly -- and I can quote from page 31106 for the benefit of my colleague where he says at the end: "However, I was thinking logically since he had not reacted to my report sent on the 15th, since in the course of the conversation that we conducted on the morning of the 17th, since never happened after my report on the 16th, I fully believed that he was in possession of certain information." That's one of the references I referred -- I use in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my colleague can use more during his re-direct if he wants, but I can come back with more on Monday morning. I'd like to have an answer though, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Not to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll come to that on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will finish here for today, and we come to that on Monday. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I do this really at other people's invitation, but I would like to invite you to consider time-tabling. I've been collating the various estimates of my colleagues for the amount of time they will require for cross-examination of Mr. Pandurevic. You may or may not know that it's my conclusion that his evidence will take this month, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The way I have worked it out, Mr. Haynes, on the basis of 50 hours, is that this will take us probably at most until the 4th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I think my estimate is a little more optimistic, I think I got it to pretty much the end of February. You might recall that I mentioned that I would appreciate, and I think everybody else would appreciate the opportunity of taking stock at the end of his evidence to see what shape the rest of my case would take; and I wondered whether at this point in the proceedings you'd actually reached any firm conclusions about that, and that's all I really wanted to open for discussion now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Haynes, we have not yet come to a conclusion particularly it seems because when you mentioned this matter in the beginning of your direct, you had indicated that you would require something like a week. So perhaps you will think about it and tell us on Monday whether you still maintain that you will require a week, and then we'll be in a position to tell you what our intentions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I'll come back to you on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We stand adjourned until Monday morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 16th day of February, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.
